topic: Measure: process maps, data, sampling and measurement systems

notes.front: What is a process map?
notes.back: A flow-chart picture of a process, split into its individual steps, decisions and inputs.
notes.explanation: Breaking the process into its component steps lets a team understand it one step at a time.
notes.example: Like a recipe drawn as boxes and arrows: take order, check stock, pack, ship, with a diamond where stock might be missing.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Process Map”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a swim-lane map, what is a swim lane?
notes.back: One of the individually defined rows into which a process map is divided.
notes.explanation: The map still shows the process steps; swim lanes add a set of separately defined rows to hold them.
notes.example: Like the lanes of a running track: each lane is its own row, and the work crosses from lane to lane as it moves on.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Swim Lanes”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a spaghetti map show?
notes.back: The physical movement of people or things within a process, drawn as a picture.
notes.explanation: A process map traces steps and decisions; a spaghetti map traces where things physically travel.
notes.example: Like tracing with a pen every walk a nurse makes between ward, store room and desk during one shift.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Spaghetti Map”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What makes an activity value-added?
notes.back: It changes the form, fit or function of the product in a way the customer needs.
notes.explanation: The test is what happens to the product: an activity that leaves it unchanged adds no value in this sense.
notes.example: Like drilling the holes a customer ordered in a bracket; carrying the bracket to a shelf changes nothing about it.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Value Add”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a non-value-added activity?
notes.back: Any activity that adds no form, feature or function to the product; LeanOhio lists transport, storage and queues among others.
notes.explanation: Machine repairs, inventory and handling are also on LeanOhio's list: time and effort are spent but the product is unchanged.
notes.example: Like a finished order waiting in a tray for a signature: time passes, but the order itself does not change.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Non-Value Add”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a non-value-added but necessary activity?
notes.back: An activity that adds no form, feature or function, yet must be done because a mandate, law or code requires it.
notes.explanation: It fails the value-added test, yet the mandate, law or code behind it means it cannot simply be dropped.
notes.example: Like a building-code inspection of wiring before walls are closed: the house is no different for it, but the step is compulsory.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Non-Value Add but Necessary”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an operational definition?
notes.back: An exact description of a characteristic and of how, specifically, data collectors are to measure it.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio says it removes ambiguity so every collector has the same understanding, cutting the chance of different results between collectors.
notes.example: Like defining "late delivery" as "signed for more than 15 minutes after the booked slot, timed by the driver's scanner" rather than just "late".
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Operational Definitions”, p. 10
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a data collection plan for?
notes.back: Planning how data will be prepared and collected, for example during a process improvement project.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio gives the aims of collecting data as keeping information on record, making decisions on important issues and passing information to others.
notes.example: Like a one-page table agreed before measuring starts: what will be counted, by whom, how often and where the results go.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Data Collection Plan”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a check sheet?
notes.back: A form for recording quantitative or qualitative data in real time, laid out so each entry falls into a category as it is recorded.
notes.explanation: It is designed with operational definitions, which is what allows entries to be sorted into categories at the moment they are made.
notes.example: Like a tally grid beside a help-desk phone, with one column per complaint type, ticked as each call comes in.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Check Sheet”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is continuous data?
notes.back: Data from a measurement system that can give an infinite number of possible values.
notes.explanation: Its possible values cannot all be listed, which is the difference LeanOhio draws from discrete data.
notes.example: Like the length of a phone call in seconds, which could be 62.4 or 62.41 or anything in between.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Continuous Data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is discrete data?
notes.back: Data from a measurement system that can give only a finite number of possible values.
notes.explanation: Its possible values can be counted off in full, unlike continuous data.
notes.example: Like a pass or fail verdict, or a rating on a 1-to-5 scale.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Discrete Data”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Stevens's typology, what are the four levels of measurement?
notes.back: Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio: four scale types Stevens proposed in 1946.
notes.explanation: Stevens meant the four scales to unify qualitative data (the nominal type) and quantitative data (the other types).
notes.example: Like sorting defects by type, ranking them minor to critical, logging oven temperature in degrees Celsius and weighing parts in grams: four different kinds of scale.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: Stevens claimed that all measurement in science was conducted using four different types of scales that he called "nominal", "ordinal", "interval", and "ratio", unifying both " qualitative " (which are described by his "nominal" type) and " quantitative "

notes.front: What is a sampling method, and what makes it a probability sampling method?
notes.back: A way of choosing which units of a population enter the sample; in probability sampling every unit has a known chance above zero.
notes.explanation: The source says these two traits together make it possible to produce unbiased estimates of population totals.
notes.example: Like drawing names from a hat that holds every employee, where each name's chance can be worked out in advance.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Sampling (statistics)”, “Probability and nonprobability sampling” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: probability sample is a sample in which every unit in the population has a chance (greater than zero) of being selected in the sample, and this probability can be accurately determined. The combination of these traits makes it possible to produce unbiased estimates of population totals

notes.front: What is a simple random sample?
notes.back: A sample in which every subset of the given size from the sampling frame has an equal chance of selection, so every element does too.
notes.explanation: The frame is not subdivided or partitioned; equal chances for every subset carry through to every single element.
notes.example: Like numbering all 800 batch records and letting a random-number generator choose 40 of them.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: In a simple random sample (SRS) of a given size, all subsets of a sampling frame have an equal probability of being selected. Each element of the frame thus has an equal probability of selection: the frame is not subdivided or partitioned.

notes.front: What is a stratified sample?
notes.back: A sample taken by organising the frame into its distinct categories (strata) and sampling each stratum as an independent sub-population.
notes.explanation: Within each stratum, individual elements can be selected at random, so every category is represented by design.
notes.example: Like drawing 10 insurance claims at random from each of three regional offices rather than 30 from one combined pile.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: When the population embraces a number of distinct categories, the frame can be organized by these categories into separate "strata." Each stratum is then sampled as an independent sub-population, out of which individual elements can be randomly selected.

notes.front: What is a cluster sample?
notes.back: A sample that selects respondents in groups (clusters), which are often defined by geography or by time period.
notes.explanation: The source gives cost as the motive: selecting in groups can be more cost-effective than selecting individuals.
notes.example: Like choosing 5 of a firm's 60 branch offices at random and surveying everyone who works in those five.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: Sometimes it is more cost-effective to select respondents in groups ('clusters'). Sampling is often clustered by geography or by time periods

notes.front: What is a systematic sample?
notes.back: A sample taken from an ordered list by starting at a random point and then selecting every kth element.
notes.explanation: The interval k is the population size divided by the sample size, and the start is chosen at random.
notes.example: Like checking every 25th parcel on a conveyor after a randomly chosen first parcel.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: Systematic sampling involves a random start and then proceeds with the selection of every k th element from then onwards. In this case, k =(population size/sample size).

notes.front: What is convenience sampling?
notes.back: A non-probability method that draws the sample from whichever part of the population is close to hand.
notes.explanation: The source also calls it accidental, grab or opportunity sampling, and classes it as non-probability sampling.
notes.example: Like timing only the calls taken by the agents who happen to sit nearest the analyst's desk.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: Accidental sampling (sometimes known as grab , convenience , or opportunity sampling ) is a type of nonprobability sampling which involves the sample being drawn from that part of the population which is close to hand.

notes.front: When data are charted in subgroups, what does MoreSteam say one subgroup should contain?
notes.back: Items measured together: at the same time and under the same conditions.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam's tool labels each subgroup in the data (the first five parts 1, the next five 2) and needs all subgroups the same size for its analysis. This deck calls such a group a rational subgroup; the cited page says only “subgroup”.
notes.example: Like measuring three bottles from a filler at the top of each hour: each hour's three bottles form one subgroup.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is measurement system analysis (MSA) for?
notes.back: Qualifying a measurement system for use by quantifying its accuracy, precision and stability.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam's reasoning: when decisions rest on measurements, more error in the measurements means more error in the decisions.
notes.example: Like checking that a kitchen thermometer reads true, and reads the same twice, before trusting it to decide when meat is cooked.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a gauge R&R (GR&R) study for?
notes.back: Characterising how well gauges and instruments used in production perform, in terms of the errors that affect their measurements.
notes.explanation: It looks at gauges in the production setting where they are actually used. This deck spells it "gauge", as the handbook does; many texts write "gage".
notes.example: Like having three inspectors each measure the same ten shafts twice with one micrometer, and then working out how much of the spread comes from the gauge and the inspectors.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.4 “Gauge R & R studies”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: The purpose of this section is to outline the steps that can be taken to characterize the performance of gauges and instruments used in a production setting in terms of errors that affect the measurements.

notes.front: In measurement system analysis, what does repeatability assess?
notes.back: Whether one appraiser, measuring the same part several times with the same device, gets the same value.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam groups it with reproducibility under the spread of measurement values, that is, precision.
notes.example: Like one lab technician weighing the same sample five times on one balance and seeing how far the readings differ.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In measurement system analysis, what does reproducibility assess?
notes.back: Whether different appraisers, measuring the same part with the same device, get the same value.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam groups it with repeatability under the spread of measurement values (precision): repeatability is one appraiser measuring again, reproducibility is different appraisers.
notes.example: Like three shift inspectors each measuring one reference pin with a shared calliper and comparing their results.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In measurement, what is bias?
notes.back: The difference between the average of measurements made on the same object and its true value.
notes.explanation: It is a quantitative term: a number found from the average of repeated measurements, set against the true value.
notes.example: Like a scale that averages 502 g when weighing a certified 500 g mass: its bias is +2 g.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.1.1.3 “Bias and Accuracy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Bias is a quantitative term describing the difference between the average of measurements made on the same object and its true value.

notes.front: What is the resolution of a measurement system?
notes.back: Its ability to detect and faithfully indicate small changes in the characteristic being measured.
notes.explanation: The definition has two parts: the system must both detect a small change and indicate it faithfully.
notes.example: Like a ruler marked only in whole centimetres, which cannot show that one part is 2 mm longer than another.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: is the ability of the measurement system to detect and faithfully indicate small changes in the characteristic of the measurement result.

notes.front: In the handbook's gauge studies, what does linearity mean?
notes.back: Gauge response rises in equal increments for equal increments of stimulus; or, if the gauge is biased, the bias stays constant.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this a narrow interpretation of linearity, chosen for its gauge studies.
notes.example: Like a scale that reads 0.2 kg low at 10 kg but 3 kg low at 100 kg: its bias changes across the range, so it is not linear in this sense.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.4.5.2 “Linearity of the gauge”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Linearity is given a narrow interpretation in this Handbook to indicate that gauge response increases in equal increments to equal increments of stimulus, or, if the gauge is biased, that the bias remains constant throughout the course of the measurement process.

notes.front: What is drift in a gauge?
notes.back: A slow change in the response of a gauge.
notes.explanation: For comparator measurements, the handbook says short-term drift is frequently caused by heat building up in the instrument while it measures.
notes.example: Like a pressure sensor whose reading on the same reference creeps up a little each week.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Drift can be defined ( VIM ) as a slow change in the response of a gauge. Instruments used as comparators for calibration Short-term drift can be a problem for comparator measurements. The cause is frequently heat build-up in the instrument during the time of measurement.

notes.front: What does attribute agreement analysis measure?
notes.back: Agreement within each appraiser's repeated judgements, between appraisers, and between appraisers and a reference standard.
notes.explanation: It is the measurement system analysis used when appraisers make judgements such as pass or fail; MoreSteam's tool reports percent agreement for each comparison.
notes.example: Like three inspectors each grading the same 30 weld photos as good or bad, twice, and comparing their grades with an expert's.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A pharmacy must make a signed register entry for every controlled drug it dispenses, because the law requires it. The medicine itself is unchanged. How is the entry classed?
notes.back: D) Non-value-added but necessary.
notes.choices:
A) Value-added activity
B) Non-value-added activity that should simply be removed
C) Value-added, because a law requires it
D) Non-value-added but necessary
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing about the medicine's form, feature or function changes. B: the step cannot just be removed while the law requires it. C: a legal requirement does not make a step value-added.
notes.explanation: The step adds no form, feature or function, and it is required by law, which is exactly LeanOhio's description of this class.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Non-Value Add but Necessary”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants to show how far forklift drivers travel across a warehouse floor during a shift. Which picture fits best?
notes.back: A) Spaghetti map.
notes.choices:
A) Spaghetti map
B) Swim-lane map
C) SIPOC
D) Check sheet
notes.choicesExplained: B: swim lanes sort a process map's steps into rows; they do not trace physical travel. C: a SIPOC does not trace physical movement. D: a check sheet records data in categories.
notes.explanation: The question is about physical movement, which is what a spaghetti map pictures.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Spaghetti Map”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A service team records four measures. Which one is discrete data?
notes.back: B) Whether each form passes or fails review.
notes.choices:
A) The fill weight of each bottle in grams
B) Whether each form passes or fails review
C) The time each caller waits, in seconds
D) The temperature of each oven at noon
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are measured on scales where any value within a range is possible, so each has infinitely many possible outcomes: continuous data.
notes.explanation: A pass-or-fail verdict has a finite number of possible outcomes (two), which is LeanOhio's test for discrete data.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Discrete Data”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On Stevens's nominal scale, what relationship between the classes can be relied on?
notes.back: None. The scale holds only distinct classes or categories, so measuring with it is the same as classifying.
notes.explanation: With no relationship between classes to rely on, placing an item on the scale amounts to putting it in a class.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Level of measurement”, “Nominal scale” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: A nominal scale consists only of a number of distinct classes or categories, for example: [Cat, Dog, Rabbit]. Unlike the other scales, no kind of relationship between the classes can be relied upon. Thus measuring with the nominal scale is equivalent to classifying .

notes.front: What does Stevens's ordinal scale allow that the nominal scale does not, and what does it still not allow?
notes.back: It allows rank order, so data can be sorted; it still does not allow the relative degree of difference between ranks.
notes.explanation: Ranks such as 1st, 2nd and 3rd can be put in order, but how far apart they are is not something the scale can tell you.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Level of measurement”, “Ordinal scale” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The ordinal type allows for rank order (1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.) by which data can be sorted but still does not allow for a relative degree of difference between them.

notes.front: What can Stevens's interval scale express that the ordinal scale cannot, and what can it still not express?
notes.back: The degree of difference between measurements, but not the ratio between them.
notes.explanation: Temperature on the Celsius scale is the source's first example: differences in degrees can be compared, ratios cannot.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Level of measurement”, “Interval scale” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The interval type allows for defining the degree of difference between measurements, but not the ratio between measurements. Examples include temperature scales with the Celsius scale

notes.front: On which of Stevens's scales can two measurements be compared by division, as with mass, length and duration?
notes.back: The ratio scale.
notes.explanation: Unlike the interval scale, ratios can be compared by division, and most measurement in the physical sciences and engineering is done on ratio scales.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Level of measurement”, “Ratio scale” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: Most measurement in the physical sciences and engineering is done on ratio scales. Examples include mass , length , duration , plane angle , energy and electric charge . In contrast to interval scales, ratios can be compared using division .

notes.front: An emergency department labels each patient priority 1, 2, 3 or 4 by urgency. The labels can be put in order, but nobody claims the gap between 1 and 2 equals the gap between 3 and 4. Which level of measurement is this?
notes.back: C) Ordinal.
notes.choices:
A) Nominal
B) Ratio
C) Ordinal
D) Interval
notes.choicesExplained: A: nominal classes have no order, yet these labels do. B: a ratio scale would allow comparison by division. D: an interval scale would make the differences between levels meaningful.
notes.explanation: Rank order without a meaningful degree of difference between ranks is what defines the ordinal scale.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Level of measurement”, “Ordinal scale” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The ordinal type allows for rank order (1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.) by which data can be sorted but still does not allow for a relative degree of difference between them.

notes.front: In statistics, how does a population differ from a sample?
notes.back: The population is the whole set of items of interest; a sample is a subset of it, analysed to estimate the population's parameters.
notes.explanation: Sample statistics are the estimates and population parameters are what they estimate: a statistic describes the sample, a parameter the population.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: By analyzing a subset of the population , it is then possible to estimate the population parameters using the appropriate sample statistics .

notes.front: When is systematic sampling especially likely to give an unrepresentative sample?
notes.back: When the list has a periodic pattern whose period is a multiple or factor of the sampling interval.
notes.explanation: In that case the source says the scheme can end up less accurate than simple random sampling.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: However, systematic sampling is especially vulnerable to periodicities in the list. If periodicity is present and the period is a multiple or factor of the interval used, the sample is especially likely to be un representative of the overall population, making the scheme less accurate than simple random sampling.

notes.front: A call centre runs three shifts whose handling times are thought to differ. An analyst randomly picks 20 calls from each shift's log. Which sampling method is this?
notes.back: D) Stratified sample.
notes.choices:
A) Convenience sampling
B) Cluster sample
C) Systematic sample
D) Stratified sample
notes.choicesExplained: B: a cluster sample would take whole groups and study the units in them, not a random draw within every group. C: there is no ordered list with every kth call taken. A: the calls are picked at random, not because they are close to hand.
notes.explanation: The shifts are the distinct categories (strata), and each one is sampled as its own sub-population with random selection inside it.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: When the population embraces a number of distinct categories, the frame can be organized by these categories into separate "strata." Each stratum is then sampled as an independent sub-population, out of which individual elements can be randomly selected.

notes.front: To save time, an analyst times only the orders packed at the bench nearest her office and uses them to describe the whole packing area. Which sampling method is this?
notes.back: D) Convenience sampling.
notes.choices:
A) Simple random sample
B) Systematic sample
C) Stratified sample
D) Convenience sampling
notes.choicesExplained: A: not every subset of orders had an equal chance of selection. B: there is no random start and fixed interval through an ordered list. C: the packing area was not split into categories each sampled at random.
notes.explanation: The sample comes from the part of the population that was close to hand, and the source warns such a sample cannot support scientific generalisation to the whole population.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The researcher using such a sample cannot scientifically make generalizations about the total population from this sample because it would not be representative enough.

notes.front: What is sampling bias?
notes.back: Collecting a sample so that some members of the intended population have a lower or higher chance of selection than others.
notes.explanation: The result is a biased sample in which not every individual was equally likely to be selected.
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: sampling bias is a bias in which a sample is collected in such a way that some members of the intended population have a lower or higher sampling probability than others. It results in a biased sample [ 1 ] of a population (or non-human factors) in which all individuals, or instances, were not equally likely to have been selected.

notes.front: A supervisor records a single pH reading from a tank every hour and wants to chart the data in subgroups. What subgroup size should she enter?
notes.choices:
A) 24, one day's readings
B) 1
C) 60, the minutes in each hour
D) The data cannot be put in subgroups
notes.choicesExplained: A: the readings were not taken together at the same time. C: only one item is measured in each hour. D: MoreSteam's tool accepts a subgroup size of one when a single item is measured per period.
notes.explanation: A subgroup holds the items measured together at the same time and under the same conditions; here that is one reading per hour.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: MoreSteam describes a measurement system by location and by spread (precision). Which characteristics fall under each?
notes.back: Location: stability, bias and linearity. Spread (precision): repeatability and reproducibility.
notes.explanation: Location compares the average measured value with the actual value; spread is about how far repeated measurements scatter.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the handbook distinguish accuracy from bias?
notes.back: Accuracy is qualitative: whether a measurement agrees with the true value. Bias is quantitative: the average measurement minus the true value.
notes.explanation: One is a judgement about agreement; the other is a number calculated from the average of repeated measurements.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.1.1.3 “Bias and Accuracy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Accuracy is a qualitative term referring to whether there is agreement between a measurement made on an object and its true (target or reference) value. Bias is a quantitative term describing the difference between the average of measurements made on the same object and its true value.

notes.front: Can bias remain in a measurement process when all equipment and standards are properly calibrated?
notes.back: Yes. Errors contributing to bias can remain; temperature probably has the most potential to introduce such bias.
notes.explanation: The handbook's example is a constant heat source, which will introduce serious errors in dimensional measurements of metal objects.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.1.1.3 “Bias and Accuracy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Errors that contribute to bias can be present even where all equipment and standards are properly calibrated and under control. Temperature probably has the most potential for introducing this type of bias into the measurements. For example, a constant heat source will introduce serious errors in dimensional measurements of metal objects.

notes.front: What rule of thumb does MoreSteam give for the resolution a measurement system needs?
notes.back: At least one-tenth of the smaller of the specification tolerance and the process spread.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam's reason: if resolution is too coarse, the measurement system will not recognise the process's variability.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On MoreSteam's % contribution basis (each source's share of the total variation), when is a gauge R&R result acceptable, possibly acceptable, or not acceptable?
notes.back: Up to 1%: acceptable. Over 1% up to 9%: may be acceptable on other grounds. Over 9%: not acceptable.
notes.explanation: On this basis repeatability, reproducibility and part-to-part variation are true shares of the total, so together they add up to 100%.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the gauge R&R bands MoreSteam quotes for % study variation and % tolerance differ from its % contribution bands?
notes.back: They are 10% and 30%, not 1% and 9%: up to 10% acceptable, 10–30% possibly acceptable, over 30% not acceptable.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam warns that these columns are not true shares of the total: their components do not add up to 100%, so the values need care.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A gauge R&R study shows that repeatability and reproducibility together make up 6% of the total variation on MoreSteam's % contribution basis. On its bands for that basis, what follows?
notes.back: C) It may be acceptable, depending on considerations such as cost and application.
notes.choices:
A) The measurement system is acceptable outright
B) The measurement system is not acceptable
C) It may be acceptable, depending on considerations such as cost and application
D) The study is invalid because the result is below 10%
notes.choicesExplained: A: outright acceptance needs 1% or less. B: rejection starts above 9%. D: 10% is a band limit on the study-variation basis, not a validity test for a % contribution result.
notes.explanation: 6% sits in the band above 1% and up to 9%, where the decision turns on other considerations such as the cost of switching or the type of application.

notes.front: In a good gauge R&R study, which component of variation should be the largest?
notes.back: Part-to-part variation.
notes.explanation: In MoreSteam's components-of-variation chart the tallest bars should belong to part-to-part variation, meaning that variation among parts is the biggest component.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A gauge R&R study shows too much measurement error, and repeatability is by far the largest contributor. Where does MoreSteam say improvement should start?
notes.back: B) Improve the measuring equipment.
notes.choices:
A) Retrain the appraisers in the procedure
B) Improve the measuring equipment
C) Choose parts that vary less
D) Add more appraisers to the study
notes.choicesExplained: A: training and procedure are MoreSteam's remedy when reproducibility is the largest source. C: parts should represent the whole process spread; narrower parts would overstate gauge error. D: more appraisers does not reduce one appraiser's scatter on repeat measurements.
notes.explanation: Repeatability is the same appraiser getting different values on the same part with the same device, which points to the equipment.

notes.front: Four inspectors judge each weld as "accept" or "reject", and the team wants to know whether they agree with themselves, with each other and with an expert. Which study fits?
notes.back: A) Attribute agreement analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Attribute agreement analysis
B) A drift study
C) A resolution check
D) A linearity study
notes.choicesExplained: D: linearity concerns whether a gauge's bias stays constant across its range. B: drift is a slow change in a gauge's response. C: resolution concerns detecting small changes in a measured value.
notes.explanation: The three comparisons asked for (within an appraiser, between appraisers, and against a standard) are exactly what attribute agreement analysis quantifies.
